## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview:** Guzik opens with Morgan's view that this psalm shows how the very things that attack faith can become a reason to praise God in worship. [EW]

**v. 1:**
- Vengeance belongs to God and not to people. God sees and knows more than we do, so it is right to ask Him to act and to trust His timing. [EW]
- Clarke separates God's justice, which gives everyone what they are due, from human revenge, which comes from angry feelings. Boice quotes Samuel Johnson: revenge comes from passion, vengeance from justice. [EW]
- The repeated words tie God's vengeance to His glory ("shine forth"). VanGemeren reads "shine forth" as a prayer for God to appear in royal splendour and bring justice. [EW]
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is shorter and sharper ("God of retributions… shine forth"). Repeating a phrase for emphasis is a feature of this psalm, as in vv. 3 and 23. [ELL]

**v. 2:**
- "Rise up" (KJV "lift up thyself") means either "be exalted" or "rise to pass sentence." [ELL]
- The psalmist leaves vengeance to God but still asks Him to do His work as Judge. Spurgeon and Maclaren argue that wanting justice is right when it comes from love of what is right and pity for victims, not from personal revenge. [EW]

**v. 3:**
- "How long?" is both bold and humble, like the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:9–10. [EW]
- Kidner: the only question is *how long*. God is not blind and has made no deal with darkness; the night is simply long. Spurgeon notes that this cry has risen from dungeons and from the whipping-posts of slavery. [EW]

**v. 4:**
- The wicked are known first by their insolent, boastful words. The righteous, by contrast, speak humbly. [EW]
- Ellicott renders it "they speak out of utter impudence." Modern scholars link the Hebrew word for "boast" to the Arabic title *Emir*. The idea is that they act like great men or lord it over God's people. [ELL]

**v. 5:**
- The wicked are known next by what they do to God's people, His "heritage." Kidner: these tyrants need not be foreigners; they could be home-grown, like King Manasseh. [EW]
- "Break in pieces" means "crush." Compare Isaiah 3:15, where the same word is paired with grinding the faces of the poor. [ELL]

**v. 6:**
- The wicked attack the weak, even to the point of murder. The righteous care for the weak. [EW]
- The mention of the "stranger" (the friendless foreigner, Exodus 22:21) suggests the oppressors are Israel's own rulers, not a foreign power. [ELL]

**v. 7:**
- The wicked think God is blind, and that belief leads them to arrogance. Spurgeon: they acted blindly because they imagined a blind God. Poole thinks "God of Jacob" is said with sarcasm. [EW]
- The Hebrew name here is "Jah." Ellicott says the idea of gods who don't care was common in ancient philosophy, and points to Seneca, Lucretius and the Homeric hymns. [ELL]

**v. 8:**
- "Senseless" means "brutish," as in Psalm 92:6. Poole: people who think themselves wise but are really the most brutish. [EW]
- Ellicott reads vv. 8–10 as proof of God's providence from both nature and history. He says the argument works against modern atheism too: life and conscience point to a mind that existed first. [ELL]

**v. 9:**
- The argument is simple: the Maker of ears and eyes must be able to hear and see. Kidner says the logic can't be escaped once you accept that God made us. [EW]
- Clarke notes the psalm doesn't say God *has* ears or eyes, only that He hears and sees. It avoids picturing God with a body. [EW]

**v. 10:**
- "Chastiseth" can also mean "instructeth." Ellicott says this partly looks ahead to Paul's teaching in Romans 1 that God teaches the nations. [ELL]

**v. 11:**
- Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 3:20 and echoes it in Romans 1:21. [EW]
- The Hebrew could mean "for *they* (mankind) are a breath," not "the thoughts are vanity." But the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads it as the KJV does, and that is how Paul quotes it, with "the wise" in place of "man." [ELL]

**v. 12:**
- Kidner: here the pupil is speaking, not the teacher. It is a triumph of faith in the middle of trouble. Brooks: discipline only makes a person blessed when God teaches through it. [EW]
- Ellicott sees a higher note than complaint here. The Old Testament could not fully explain how suffering can be a blessing, though Job comes close. [ELL]

**v. 13:**
- Those taught by God's word have rest when hard days come. Maclaren: you can have rest in the middle of evil if you understand its purpose. Trapp reads the "pit" as the grave and hell. [EW]
- "Rest" probably means being calmed while watching God's providence at work. Without the next clause it would more naturally mean "deliver him from evil days." For the pit, compare Psalm 9:15. [ELL]

**v. 14:**
- This promise was given to Israel and extends to believers. Spurgeon: God has no cast-offs. [EW]

**v. 15:**
- Literally, "to righteousness judgment shall turn." The apparent contradiction between God's justice and what we see will end. "Follow it" is a common Hebrew phrase for loyalty to a cause, especially loyalty to the LORD. Ellicott quotes Luther's paraphrase on right staying right. [ELL]
- Trapp: everything will be set right, at the last judgment if not before (Romans 2:6–10). [EW]

**v. 16:**
- "Rise up" means stand up as a champion. Compare Shammah's stand in 2 Samuel 23:11. [ELL]
- The psalmist admits his own limits while the day of justice has not yet come. [EW]

**v. 17:**
- "Silence" means the grave (compare Psalm 31:17). [ELL]
- VanGemeren: the psalmist nearly slipped away into the world of the dead. Spurgeon: having no human helper makes God dearer to us. [EW]

**v. 18:**
- Clarke: "hold me up" pictures propping up something that is falling. God's mercy keeps weak believers from ruin. [EW]

**v. 19:**
- "Thoughts" literally means "divided" thoughts, that is, anxious ones. The Septuagint and Latin Vulgate have "griefs." [ELL]
- "Delight" literally means to stroke or soothe. In Isaiah 66:11 the word describes a mother calming her child. [ELL]
- Poole: the anxious thoughts include fears about one's future state. [EW]

**v. 20:**
- A "throne of iniquity" means an unjust government. The word could mean "calamity," but "lawless desire" fits best here. The question is whether God's rule could ever take such rulers as partners. "By a law" means using laws to do wrong; some translate it "against the law" instead. [ELL]
- Maclaren and Spurgeon both condemn using legal forms to cover injustice. Guzik links the verse to 1 John 1:6. [EW]

**v. 21:**
- This may mean crowding into the law courts to condemn the innocent, or attacking the righteous more generally. The Septuagint has "they hunt." [ELL]
- Clarke: evil people are always united in evil. [EW]

**v. 22:**
- Boice: here the writer gives his own testimony that what he promised others has proved true for him. [EW]

**v. 23:**
- The punishment fits the crime: those who cut off others are cut off themselves. The repeated "cut them off" matches the repeated "vengeance" in v. 1. [EW]
- Spurgeon: sin itself is the punishment of sin, because each sin makes the next more likely. [EW]

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I didn't find any real disagreement between traditions in what I read. The teachers Guzik quotes come from several traditions (Spurgeon and Maclaren, Baptist; Clarke, Methodist; Kidner, Anglican; Boice, Presbyterian), and they agree on this psalm. The only debate I saw is at **v. 14**: Guzik mentions that some teach God *did* cast off Israel, and he argues this verse contradicts that view. He doesn't say who holds it. [EW]

## 3. Other views

- **Modern scholarship:** The only points I found are Ellicott's notes citing "modern scholars" and alternative readings of the Hebrew at vv. 4, 11 and 20. [ELL]
- **Not covered:** I found no Catholic, Orthodox, NET Bible notes or prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace material.
